subsection: 6. Eggs: selection, storage, properties and culinary uses

notes.h: Selecting eggs and reading the labelling
notes.b: Eggs are a fresh, perishable food, so choosing well and reading the carton tells you how safe, fresh and traceable they are. Most of what a buyer needs to know is printed on the carton or stamped on the egg.
points: Choose eggs with clean, unbroken shells from a clean shop, because a cracked shell lets bacteria in. Eggs sold as Class A are not washed.
Eggs are graded by class and by size, which is small, medium or large (and extra large). Shop eggs are Class A.
Check the best-before date on the carton, and use the eggs by it. It is set at no more than 28 days after the egg was laid.
The carton shows the country of origin, and the name, address and registration number of the producer or packer. It also shows the week number (the week the eggs were packed), the class and the size.

The farming method is stated: organic, free-range, barn or caged. Methods differ in animal welfare and price, while nutrition is much the same, though free-range eggs may contain more of some vitamins (B12, niacin).

Each egg is stamped with a producer code, so it can be traced back to its farm and county. The first digit gives the method of production (0 organic, 1 free-range, 2 barn, 3 caged), then IE for Ireland, then a code for the producer.
The Bord Bia Quality Assurance mark confirms that the producer meets its requirements. Many Irish eggs carry it.

Labels must be clear, legible, indelible and not misleading, under Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 as given effect in Ireland. Organic eggs come from hens reared to organic standards, with no routine antibiotic or growth-hormone treatment and feed free of artificial pesticides and fertilisers.
notes.tip: For a question on labelling, name several items from the carton (origin, producer or packer, class, size, week number, date, farming method, storage), the egg stamp for traceability and the Bord Bia mark, and say the label must be clear and not misleading. Write best-before, not use-by, for eggs. Free-range or organic eggs are not safer without quality assurance.

notes.b: Salmonella (a food poisoning bacterium) can be in a hen's gut and, rarely, in the egg itself. Controlling it on the farm lowers the risk of food poisoning, so egg producers follow a quality assurance scheme.
points: Ireland has an EU-approved national salmonella control plan for laying hens, to keep the national flock healthy and the eggs safe.
Incoming hens (young hens, called pullets) must be certified as salmonella free, so infection is not brought onto the farm.
Laying hens are checked for salmonella each month, so any infection is found early.
All feed for laying hens is heat-treated, which kills bacteria in the feed.
Management systems ensure full traceability of every egg, so a problem egg can be tracked back to its source.
All producers and suppliers are inspected and approved.
Every system is independently inspected before the Bord Bia Quality mark is awarded, so the mark shows the checks have been passed.
notes.tip: A question on quality assurance looks for five or six separate points: the salmonella control plan, certified hens, monthly testing, heat-treated feed, traceability, inspection and the Bord Bia mark.

notes.b: An egg's shell is porous and its quality falls as it ages, so good storage keeps it fresh and safe. The rules follow from the shell and the egg's inner structure.
points: Store eggs in the fridge at 4°C, in the egg compartment rather than the door, because the door is warmer and the eggs are shaken each time it opens.
Store them pointed end down, away from strongly flavoured foods, because the shell is porous and the eggs absorb smells. Keep them away from cooked foods.
Do not wash the shell, because washing removes the protective cuticle (the thin natural coating) and speeds staling.
Use eggs within the best-before date.
Leftover egg white can be kept in a sealed container in the fridge for 2 to 4 days.
Leftover egg yolk can be kept covered with water in a sealed container for up to 4 days.

Wash hands after handling raw eggs. Do not use cracked or dirty eggs in foods that are not cooked, and cook eggs until firm for vulnerable groups, because raw egg dishes such as mayonnaise and mousse carry a risk.
A fresh egg sinks and lies flat in water because its air cell is small, while an old egg tilts or floats. A fresh egg also has a thick white and a high, round yolk.
notes.tip: A storing-eggs question expects: fridge at 4°C, egg compartment, pointed end down, away from strong flavours, do not wash, use by the best-before date, and how to store leftover white and yolk.

notes.b: Coagulation is the setting of egg protein when heated, which thickens and binds food. It is why a runny egg becomes solid when cooked.
points: Egg white coagulates at about 60 to 65°C; egg yolk coagulates at about 65 to 70°C.
The protein chains untwist, or denature, and straighten, then bond together around small pockets of water, which traps the water so the egg sets.
Overheating makes the protein clump tighter and squeeze out its water, causing curdling and a tough, rubbery texture. Gentle, low heat and stirring give a creamy custard, while high heat curdles it.
Culinary uses, thickening: custards and quiche. Adding egg to a hot liquid slowly prevents lumps.
Culinary uses, binding: burgers, fishcakes, meatballs and stuffings, where the set egg holds the mixture together. Coating: egg and breadcrumbs on fish, and chicken goujons.
Culinary uses, glazing: egg wash on scones, pastry and bread gives gloss and colour. Clarifying: egg white traps solid particles in consommé.
Culinary uses, cooking as a dish: boiled, poached, scrambled, fried and baked eggs, and omelettes. Enriching: rice pudding and mashed potato.
notes.tip: Coagulation is the setting of the protein, so an egg used to glaze is coagulation, not aeration. Overheated protein curdles and turns tough, so do not say it burns.

notes.b: Aeration means trapping air in a food. Eggs do this well, which is how cakes and meringues become light.
points: Whisking or beating egg, the white especially, traps air as many small bubbles.
The heat from whisking partly unfolds (denatures) the egg protein, which forms a thin film that lines up around each air bubble and sets slightly, giving a foam.

This foam is temporary, so it should not be left standing or it collapses. It is stabilised permanently by further heating, as the protein coagulates in the oven, or by a setting agent such as gelatine. Sugar also helps stabilise it.
Whole eggs and sugar whisked together aerate sponge cakes and Swiss rolls. Egg and fat creamed together also aerate cake mixtures.
Whisked egg whites make meringues, soufflés, mousses, pavlova and the topping on lemon meringue.
For the best foam, use a clean, grease-free bowl and a whisk, because fat or yolk stops the foam forming. Use whites at room temperature and add sugar gradually.
notes.tip: Name aeration as trapped air with the protein around the bubbles, and call the foam temporary. Raw egg white will not whisk if fat or yolk is present.

notes.b: Oil and water do not mix by themselves. Egg yolk can hold them together, which is why it is used in sauces and dressings.
points: An emulsion is a permanent mixture of two liquids that do not normally mix, such as oil and vinegar, with one broken into tiny droplets spread through the other.
Lecithin, found in the yolk, is a natural emulsifier (a substance that joins liquids that would otherwise separate).
The hydrophilic (water-loving) head of the lecithin molecule attaches to water, and the hydrophobic (water-hating, oil-loving) tail attaches to oil.
This holds the oil and vinegar together and prevents them separating.
To make an emulsion, add the oil drop by drop to the yolk while whisking, because adding it too fast makes it curdle.
Culinary uses: mayonnaise (oil and vinegar), hollandaise and similar sauces (butter and lemon juice), and salad dressings.
Culinary uses: blending the fat and sugar in a cake mixture so the batter does not curdle.
notes.tip: To describe eggs as an emulsifier, give the structure of lecithin (water-loving head, oil-loving tail), say it holds liquids that normally separate in a permanent emulsion, and give a worked example such as mayonnaise or hollandaise made step by step.

notes.b: Cooking changes an egg's appearance, texture, safety and nutrients. Some changes are wanted and some are signs of overcooking.
points: Colour changes: the white turns from transparent to opaque white, as its protein coagulates (sets). The egg white becomes insoluble when heated.
Heat kills bacteria, including salmonella, so thoroughly cooked eggs are safer.
Vitamin B is lost during cooking, though most other nutrients change little.
Overcooking makes eggs tough and rubbery, and harder to digest, because the protein curdles. Digestibility is best with light cooking.
Iron in the yolk and sulphur in the white react to form a green-grey ring around the yolk of an overcooked hard-boiled egg. Cooling the egg quickly in cold water reduces it.
Different cooking methods and times give soft, medium and hard results.
notes.tip: Effects of heat questions look for: coagulation, curdling and toughness, colour change, loss of B vitamin, bacteria killed, the green ring and the white becoming insoluble. The ring comes from iron and sulphur reacting, not from overcooking the white alone.

questions.prompt: Explain how whisking egg whites produces a foam, and give one culinary use of the foam.
questions.model: Whisking traps air bubbles in the egg white. The heat from whisking partly unfolds the protein, which lines up around the bubbles and sets slightly. This forms a temporary foam. Culinary use: meringue, or a soufflé. The foam is fixed by further heating or by a setting agent such as gelatine.

questions.prompt: Explain how eggs are used in cooking for coagulation, aeration and emulsification, giving a culinary use for each property.
questions.model: Coagulation: egg protein sets when heated, at about 60 to 65°C in the white and 65 to 70°C in the yolk, as the protein chains unfold and bond around water; used for thickening custards and quiche, binding burgers, coating fish or glazing pastry; overheating causes curdling and a tough texture. Aeration: whisking traps air, the protein sets around the bubbles to form a foam that is fixed by heat or gelatine; used in sponge cakes, meringues and soufflés. Emulsification: lecithin in the yolk has a hydrophilic head attached to water and a hydrophobic tail attached to oil, holding immiscible liquids together; used in mayonnaise, hollandaise sauce or cake batters where fat and sugar are blended.
